papers.title: Talk, Judge, Cooperate: Gossip-Driven Indirect Reciprocity in Self-Interested LLM Agents
papers.how_tested: ALIGN framework: decentralized self-interested LLM agents share open-ended gossip to form reputations and decide whom to help in an indirect-reciprocity setting.
papers.finding: Gossip consistently improves indirect reciprocity and resists malicious entrants by identifying and ostracizing defectors; stronger reasoning models align better, chat models over-cooperate.

papers.title: Reputation as a Solution to Cooperation Collapse in LLM-based MASs
papers.how_tested: RepuNet: LLM agents form reputations from direct encounters and gossip, and form or sever network links based on reputation.
papers.finding: Reputation avoids cooperation collapse; emergent cooperative clusters, social isolation of exploitative agents, and a tendency to share positive rather than negative gossip.

papers.title: Emergence of Reputation-Based Cooperation in LLM Agents
papers.how_tested: Indirect-reciprocity donation game in which LLM agents observe behavioural traces and donate on a continuous scale; prompt-encoded strategies culturally evolve across generations and four LLM backends.
papers.finding: Robustness to free-rider invasion varies >10x across backends; only the stringency of defector exclusion predicts resistance, and agents stay at Image-Scoring-like discrimination rather than Leading-Eight norms.

papers.title: Cultural Evolution of Cooperation among LLM Agents
papers.how_tested: Iterated Donor Game over generations of LLM agents who can observe recipients' recent behaviour; optional costly-punishment variant.
papers.finding: Cooperation evolution differs by base model (Claude 3.5 Sonnet > Gemini 1.5 Flash > GPT-4o); only Claude used costly punishment to raise scores; high seed sensitivity.

papers.title: CoopEval: Benchmarking Cooperation-Sustaining Mechanisms and LLM Agents in Social Dilemmas
papers.how_tested: Cross-play of six LLMs in four social dilemmas under repetition (continuation prob. 0.8), reputation (first-order and higher-order history of co-players' past interactions), mediation, and contracts.
papers.finding: Contracting and mediation were most effective; repetition sustains cooperation but deteriorates with varying co-players; all mechanisms work better under evolutionary pressure; models defect in one-shot games.

papers.title: SODE: Analyzing Social Dynamics in LLM Agents
papers.how_tested: Evaluation framework with an indirect-reciprocity dimension measuring whether LLM agents condition cooperation on an opponent's public reputation score and manage their own image under public observability.
papers.finding: Instruction-tuned models show exploitable passive compliance, reasoning models over-focus on immediate gains; long-horizon framing activates reciprocity in reasoning models.

papers.title: Formal Mechanisms for Market Stability in Self-Interested Agent Societies: A Marketplace Simulation Study
papers.authors: Eugene Ng Yi Sheng et al.
papers.how_tested: 18 DeepSeek-V3 agents in a networked marketplace under eight conditions incl. Global Reputation (trust scores visible to all), Network Rewiring (severing links to defectors), top-down oracle monitoring, sanctions, contracts, mediation, judiciary.
papers.finding: Mediation best (+29% over baseline); network rewiring second; global reputation scored below the communication-only baseline; oracle monitoring slightly above baseline; costly sanctions worst.

papers.title: From Certain Doom to Survival: Agent-Driven Self-Governance in LLM Agent Societies
papers.how_tested: GovSim-SelfGovern: LLM agents author executable governance rules (catch caps, redistribution, exile/membership removal, progressive contributions), vote on them, and live under them.
papers.finding: Catch caps dominate but fail under scarcity; survival in fatal scenarios (27.5% vs 2.5%) requires fiscal reserves or membership reduction (exile); thinking voters pass exile 15x more often than non-thinking.

papers.title: Cooperate or Collapse: Emergence of Sustainable Cooperation in a Society of LLM Agents
papers.how_tested: GovSim common-pool simulation with five LLM agents; a moderator publicly discloses each agent's previous-round harvest (transparent harvest reporting) before a free-form discussion phase.
papers.finding: Most LLMs fail to sustain the resource; communication matters (overuse +22% without it). Transparency is a fixed feature, not manipulated.

papers.title: Strategic Exploitation in LLM Agent Markets: A Simulation Framework for E-Commerce Trust
papers.how_tested: TruthMarketTwin: LLM buyer and seller agents trade under asymmetric quality information, with reputation-based governance vs warrant enforcement.
papers.finding: LLM sellers autonomously exploit weaknesses in reputation-based governance; warrant enforcement reduces deception.

papers.title: Paying for Honesty Without Knowing the Truth: Reputation-Penalty Design for LLM Marketplace Agents
papers.how_tested: LLM merchant agents write product descriptions in a competitive marketplace; CARP reputation-penalty (deadband for complaint noise, state-dependent severity) limits sales of low-reputation sellers.
papers.finding: Merchants fabricate when lying is free but restrain when it costs sales; CARP plus reflection (SPARC) substantially narrows the welfare gap.

papers.title: Playing repeated games with large language models
papers.how_tested: Different LLMs play finitely repeated 2x2 games against each other, hand-coded strategies, and humans.
papers.finding: LLMs do well in PD-family games; GPT-4 is unforgiving (never cooperates again after a single opponent defection, i.e. grim-trigger-like rather than TFT) and coordinates poorly in Battle of the Sexes.

papers.title: Understanding LLM Agent Behaviours via Game Theory: Strategy Recognition, Biases and Multi-Agent Dynamics
papers.how_tested: Extends FAIRGAME: LLM agents play each other in repeated PD and 3-player PGG; trajectories classified into ALLC/ALLD/TFT/WSLS by supervised classifiers.
papers.finding: Model-dependent strategy mixes: WSLS is prominent (Llama 3.1 405B 46.5%, GPT-4o 34.1%), Mistral Large balanced incl. TFT 29.9%; language framing effects rival architecture effects.

papers.title: Will Systems of LLM Agents Cooperate: An Investigation into a Social Dilemma
papers.how_tested: LLMs generate complete IPD strategies with aggressive/cooperative/neutral dispositions, which are then run in evolutionary population simulations.
papers.finding: Different LLMs bias the relative success of aggressive vs cooperative strategies (partial: agents are LLM-written programs, not LLMs acting per round).

papers.title: LLM-augmented empirical game theoretic simulation for social-ecological systems
papers.how_tested: Compares LLM-agent and expert-guided EGTA models of irrigation/fishery governance; a Pigouvian parameter tau (0, 0.25, 1) internalizes externality costs in payoffs of 2-player and N-player CPR games.
papers.finding: Moderate Pigouvian tax (tau=0.25) in the expert-guided EGTA model was the only decentralized setting sustaining a mixed economy; prompting LLMs was less effective than parameterized payoffs (partial: tax effect shown in EGTA payoff model rather than among interacting LLM agents).

papers.title: Corrupted by Reasoning: Reasoning Language Models Become Free-Riders in Public Goods Games
papers.how_tested: SanctSim: LLM agents choose each round between a sanctioning and a sanction-free institution in a PGG, then contribute and reward/punish; others' data shown anonymized with identifiers randomized every round.
papers.finding: Traditional LLMs join the sanctioning institution and cooperate; reasoning models free-ride. No exclusion mechanism and no persistent per-agent reputation (listed here only to document seed-claim checks).

papers.title: Partner Selection for the Emergence of Cooperation in Multi-Agent Systems Using Reinforcement Learning
papers.how_tested: RL agents in an iterated PD population can choose interaction partners (partner selection) vs. random matching.
papers.finding: With partner selection, selfish learners learn to retaliate against defectors and cooperate with others, yielding a prosocial society.

papers.title: Cooperation and Reputation Dynamics with Reinforcement Learning
papers.how_tested: Q-learners in indirect-reciprocity donation games must learn both to use and to assign reputations; interventions: seeding fixed agents and introspection-based intrinsic rewards.
papers.finding: Plain Q-learning often converges to bad equilibria; combining both interventions stabilizes reputation-based cooperation even when fully decentralized.

papers.title: Bottom-Up Reputation Promotes Cooperation with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.how_tested: LR2: agents learn a cooperation policy and a reputation-assignment policy from local observations in spatial social dilemmas, without predefined norms.
papers.finding: Bottom-up reputation assignment reshapes rewards and produces strategy clustering that sustains cooperation.

papers.title: Learning to cooperate with emergent reputation via multi-agent reinforcement learning
papers.how_tested: COOPER jointly learns reputation assessment rules and reputation-based policies from environment rewards on social networks.
papers.finding: Adapts to existing reputation systems and co-players; reputation norms and cooperation co-emerge in self-play, robust across network topologies.

papers.title: Learning to Cooperate with Minimal Observability
papers.how_tested: Observer Model: RL agents learn from direct experience plus limited third-party observations; observability varied from none to one observer per game across population sizes; partner selection graphs analysed.
papers.finding: Direct experience alone fails in large societies; even minimal third-party observation yields robust cooperation.

papers.title: A multi-agent reinforcement learning model of reputation and cooperation in human groups
papers.how_tested: Clean Up public-goods task with identifiable vs anonymous conditions, run with humans and with MARL agents given an intrinsic reputation motive.
papers.finding: Humans cooperate only when identifiable; the MARL model with reputation motivation reproduces this and develops turn-taking coordination (partial: artificial-agent arm is a model of human data).

papers.title: Deconstructing Cooperation and Ostracism via Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.how_tested: Two RL agents play repeated PD, each with a cooperation policy and a network-rewiring (connect/disconnect) policy.
papers.finding: Rewiring facilitates cooperation via learned ostracism of defectors, but ostracism emerges from and then reinforces cooperation rather than causing it alone.

papers.title: Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning in Sequential Social Dilemmas
papers.how_tested: Gathering game: an agent hit twice by another's beam is removed from the game for N_tagged frames; N_tagged and apple abundance are manipulated.
papers.finding: Beam use (aggression) rises with scarcity and falls with higher conflict cost (partial: removal is a competitive attack, not a sanction for norm violation).

papers.title: Maintaining cooperation in complex social dilemmas using deep reinforcement learning
papers.how_tested: Constructs approximate Markov tit-for-tat (amTFT) deep-RL agents that are nice, provokable and forgiving in Markov social dilemmas.
papers.finding: Generalized TFT agents maintain cooperation in complex environments, theoretically and experimentally.

papers.title: Learning Reciprocity in Complex Sequential Social Dilemmas
papers.how_tested: Online RL algorithm with reciprocal behaviour toward co-players in a 2-player Markov game and 5-player intertemporal social dilemmas alongside selfish learners.
papers.finding: Reciprocating agents induce pro-social outcomes for the wider group.

papers.title: Melting Pot 2.0
papers.how_tested: Benchmark scenarios test focal MARL agents against reciprocator background bots (e.g., Coins high-/low-threshold reciprocators that defect for 100-150 steps after mismatching coins; Clean Up conditional cleaners).
papers.finding: Provides standardized tests of how focal populations respond to conditional-cooperation partners (benchmark; no single mechanism effect reported).

papers.title: LOPT: Learning Optimal Pigovian Tax in Sequential Social Dilemmas
papers.how_tested: An auxiliary tax agent learns a Pigovian tax/allowance policy that reshapes individual rewards toward social welfare in Escape Room and Cleanup.
papers.finding: LOPT significantly improves social welfare over state-of-the-art baselines.

papers.title: Adaptive Punishment for Cooperation in Mixed-Motive Games
papers.how_tested: APC: learned defection-awareness module sets punishment probability and severity according to detected defection in sequential social dilemmas.
papers.finding: Reduces costly, ineffective punishment and outperforms baselines (partial for P08-02: conditions punishment intensity on defection but never switches to reward).

notes: Excluded: Fontana et al. 'Nicer Than Humans' (arXiv 2406.13605, ICWSM 2025) - single LLM vs scripted random adversaries, fails the 2+ LLM agents criterion; FAIRGAME base paper (2504.14325) - framework/bias paper, strategy classification is in huynh2025understanding. guzmanpiedrahita2025corrupted (SanctSim) is listed with empty mechanism_ids only to document that it does NOT test P01-02/P02-01/P08-04: its setup randomizes agent identifiers every round (confirmed from arXiv HTML); it belongs under sanctioning primitives. Several 2026 arXiv preprints (horibe2026emergence, ngyisheng2026formal, rehm2026certain, lei2026strategic, yang2026paying, jung2026sode, song2026learning, tang2026adaptive) were verified only from abstract/HTML summaries via fetch; verifier should confirm details, especially ngyisheng2026formal utility figures and rehm2026certain exile statistics. Lerer 2017, Eccles 2019, LOPT confirmed from search result snippets of arXiv abs pages (not fully opened). LOPT year: arXiv 2023 / NeurIPS 2025; AAMAS 2023 extended abstract title was 'Learning Optimal "Pigovian Tax" in Sequential Social Dilemmas'. Akata: arXiv 2023, published NHB 2025; seed wording 'harsh TFT' should become 'unforgiving / grim-trigger-like'. Gaps: no LLM or MARL test of a shared allowlist/denylist (P02-03), no time-limited suspension used as a sanction (P02-02), no reward/punish regime switch (P08-02), no immutable/cryptographic audit log manipulated with interacting agents (P01-03). Leibo 2017 timed removal and tang2026adaptive are weak fits; verifier may prefer to drop them. Kolt (2024) not checked here.
